assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations of record accuracy and stability, made optical frequency metrology the leading precision-measurement tool, with uncertainties near 1e-18 and uses in relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. It is a clear, original and lasting advance in measuring accurately, which I weigh heavily as an atomic physicist.
assessment.attribution: A two-person prize is clean: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made early demonstrations; Ye's group drove the strontium clocks to the accuracy frontier. Other clock groups, ion clocks and comb developers (recognised in 2005 and 2012) are acknowledged but do not break a Katori-Ye pairing.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent laboratories confirm the performance and the field is mature; timing is good and the technology is stable and established.
uncertainties: Relative weighting of Katori and Ye versus other lattice-clock groups, and overlap with earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes, cannot be settled from memory.
Redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some of the impact is still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling between superconducting circuits and microwave photons the basis of dispersive readout, gates and error-corrected processors. It is conceptually original, transferring cavity QED to chips, and underpins much of today's superconducting quantum computing hardware.
assessment.attribution: Blais (with Girvin and colleagues) supplied the 2004 theory; Wallraff and Schoelkopf gave the first strong-coupling experiments. Devoret and others were central to related circuit work, so allocation needs care, but the three named people span theory and the two main experimental groups.
assessment.maturity: Extensively and independently reproduced and used in industry; recognition would be timely, though it follows closely on the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize and omission of Girvin from the credited names complicates fairness.
Whether it is distinct enough from the earlier cavity-QED recognition (2012) is arguable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry has delivered sensitive measurements of gravity, gradients, rotation and the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. It applies coherent light-atom manipulation to measuring small effects, which fits the view that progress is limited by what we can measure and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated early atom interferometers, Bordé gave the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer theory and geometry, and Kasevich led light-pulse gravimeters and gyroscopes. Steven Chu, a central figure in the light-pulse gravimeter, is not among the credited names, so the credit is awkward; I pick the three most foundational from the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a laboratory method and emerging commercially; the strongest fundamental-physics results from large-scale instruments are still developing.
uncertainties: Absence of Chu (already a laureate) from the credited names, and the role of Holger Müller, leave allocation uncertain.
Whether flagship precision results are decisive enough yet is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg-blockade arrays combine optical-tweezer control with strong, switchable interactions, giving programmable quantum simulators and gate-based computation with hundreds of atoms. It builds on laser cooling and trapping and is original in how it joins them.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and collaborators proposed Rydberg-blockade gate schemes, while Browaeys and Lukin led key experimental array demonstrations; the original blockade proposal also involved Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller and others. The credit set is plausible but incomplete, and Lukin appears on several candidates.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by several groups, but the field is evolving fast and error-corrected logic is only recently shown; moderately premature.
uncertainties: Credit for the original blockade proposal is not fully captured by the supplied names.
Computational advantage and fault tolerance are not yet established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene created a tunable platform for correlated insulators and superconductivity in a single material, opening moire physics with very large impact in condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands and the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group discovered the correlated insulating and superconducting states. The theory-experiment pairing is natural, though other experimental groups also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Broadly reproduced in many labs; the field is young and the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, so the timing is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled.
Experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero is not in the supplied names.
This is outside my own field, so my judgement is less well informed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision picture and its quantum theory explain high-harmonic generation and underpin attosecond science and orbital imaging. The three-step model is conceptually clear and widely used.
assessment.attribution: Corkum proposed the three-step model and Lewenstein with coworkers gave the quantum theory; a natural pair. Attosecond pulse generation was recognised in 2023, and the theory credit overlaps with a 2023 laureate's contributions, so allocation is sensitive.
assessment.maturity: Very well confirmed and widely used, but partly adjacent to an existing prize, which reduces urgency.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 prize and with other contributors to the theory.
Whether the committee regards this as a distinct discovery or part of a prior prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light surpassed the standard quantum limit in interferometers and is now routine in gravitational-wave detectors; a clean example of quantum states improving measurement.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-vacuum interferometry; Kimble and others made early squeezed-state experiments; Schnabel and Mavalvala drove its implementation in GEO600 and LIGO. With four credited names, a three-person selection leaves out Mavalvala, a real compromise.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is installed in LIGO, Virgo and GEO and is mature, but it follows closely on the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
uncertainties: Division of credit between theory, early experiments and detector implementation is difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Coherent light-matter interfaces, including single-atom cavity QED, electromagnetically induced transparency, slow light and quantum memories, underlie quantum repeaters and networks. The concepts are important and close to my own area.
assessment.attribution: Rempe, Kimble and Lukin each made decisive atom-photon interface demonstrations; attribution is reasonable but ensemble and solid-state memories involve many other groups, including rare-earth-crystal work not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed, but scalable quantum networks are not yet demonstrated; somewhat premature.
uncertainties: I have a possible conflict of interest because my research includes rare-earth-crystal quantum memories in this broader field.
The candidate is broad and may need to be split into parts.
